title: Watching change
hookLine: steps thirteen to sixteen: impermanence, fading, ceasing, letting go

cards: Try something. Listen to the next sound you hear: a car, a fridge, a bird. Listen until it stops, and notice the exact moment it ends.
Strange, isn't it? Almost all attention goes to things starting: the new message, the next episode, the plan for tomorrow. Almost none goes to things ending.
But everything ends. Every sound, every mood, every breath. The last four steps of the breathing discourse turn the whole practice toward that plain fact, and say it's where freedom is found.

teach.b: The fourth group of four is about seeing things as they really are. Step thirteen: contemplating impermanence, anicca, I will breathe in and out. Fourteen: contemplating fading away.
Fifteen: contemplating ceasing. Sixteen: contemplating letting go, relinquishment. Each goes a little deeper.
Impermanence is the plain observation: this breath is changing. It started, it's moving, it's ending.
Fading is seeing that as things change, the pull they have on you can fade too.
Ceasing is watching things actually end: the breath, the sound, the thought, gone.
And letting go is the hand opening, not because you're forced to, but because there's nothing left to cling to. The breath is the perfect teacher here. No in-breath lasts.
No out-breath can be kept. You can't save a breath for later. The Dhammapada, in Max Müller's translation, puts it in four words: "All created things perish."
It goes on to say that whoever sees this clearly grows weary of pain, and that this is the way to purity. That sounds bleak to some ears, but practitioners describe the opposite.
When you really see that everything changes, you stop gripping so hard, and something relaxes. The bad day will end. The good day will end too, which is a reason to taste it while it's here.
Every breath becomes both a beginning and an ending.
The sixteen steps start with a long breath and end with letting go, and the discourse says breathing practiced this way, all the way through, brings clear knowing and release.

how: In Buddhist breath meditation, the final steps turn attention to impermanence, the fading of attachment, ending and letting go, and many teachers use the breath's endings as the doorway.

o: seeing things arise, fade, end and be let go
tracking what has changed since yesterday
accepting that life is sad and short

games.q: the last four steps — tap the pairs.

s: seeing impermanence is meant to make you gloomy
practitioners describe the opposite: when you stop gripping, something relaxes.
the Dhammapada says all created things perish
you can save a breath for later
no in-breath lasts and no out-breath can be kept, which is why the breath is such a good teacher.

games.q: you're sitting, and a sound outside suddenly stops. what do the last four steps suggest?
o: ignore it: only the breath matters.
notice the ending, and let it go.
wish the sound would come back.
games.why: steps thirteen to sixteen turn attention to change and ending: every ending is a chance to let go.

practice: Rest your attention on endings: the small turn at the top of each in-breath, the pause at the bottom of each out-breath.

Then widen to sounds ending, sensations fading, thoughts dissolving, with nothing to do but watch things finish. On each out-breath, let something go: a bit of tension, a thought, the need to hold on.

wordCard.voice: Watching change. The last four steps: impermanence, fading, ceasing, and letting go.

orig.note: Pali: impermanent; Sanskrit anitya. The first of the three marks of existence.

carryVoice: Your line: let go. The breath shows how, every time it ends. Day one hundred and thirteen, rest well.
